reviewer.title: Machine Learning Algorithms — Modules 1–2 Comprehensive Reviewer
reviewer.description: Adaptive full-scope reviewer grounded in the supplied Module 1 Introduction to Machine Learning and Module 2 Supervised Learning materials.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the module's description of machine learning?
questions.explanation: The module describes machine learning as extracting knowledge from data and enabling computers to learn from data and experience rather than relying only on explicit task-specific programming.
choices: A field focused only on manually encoding decision rules
A field concerned with enabling computers to learn from data and experience
A method used only for storing large datasets
A visualization technique for plotting statistical data
questions.correctAnswer: A field concerned with enabling computers to learn from data and experience

questions.question: In the experience-task-performance formulation of learning, what indicates that a computer program has learned?
questions.explanation: A program learns when its performance P on tasks T improves through experience E.
choices: Its performance on the task improves with experience
It receives more explicit rules from a programmer
Its dataset contains no missing values
questions.correctAnswer: Its performance on the task improves with experience

questions.question: The module describes machine learning as a field at the intersection of statistics, artificial intelligence, and computer science.
questions.explanation: The introductory material explicitly places machine learning at the intersection of statistics, artificial intelligence, and computer science.

questions.question: Traditional rule-based algorithms rely on manually specified rules, while machine-learning systems can learn rules from training samples.
questions.explanation: The module contrasts explicit/manual rules in traditional algorithms with rules automatically learned from training data in machine learning.

source.section: Difference between ML Algo and Traditional Rule Based Algo (p. 9)

questions.question: Which sequence best represents the two broad phases shown in the module's ML process?
questions.explanation: The module separates the process into a learning phase using training data, preprocessing, learning, and testing, followed by prediction on new data using the trained model.
questions.correctAnswer: Learning followed by prediction

questions.question: The module identifies NumPy with scientific computing, Matplotlib with scientific plotting, and Pandas with data wrangling and analysis.
questions.explanation: These functions are explicitly paired with NumPy, Matplotlib, and Pandas in the module's Python tools table.

questions.question: According to the module, the prominent Python library specifically identified as a very popular tool for machine learning is ____.
questions.explanation: The module explicitly identifies Scikit-learn as a very popular tool and prominent Python library for machine learning.

questions.question: A dataset contains several absent attribute values. Which data-quality problem from the module does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The module defines incompleteness as data containing missing values or lacking attributes.
questions.correctAnswer: Incompleteness

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of data preprocessing as presented in the module?
questions.explanation: Preprocessing cleans, alters, reorganizes, and transforms raw data so that it is ready for analysis or modeling.
choices: To prepare raw data for analysis or modeling
To eliminate the need for training data
To deploy a model directly into production
questions.correctAnswer: To prepare raw data for analysis or modeling

questions.question: (Choose 3) Which activities are listed under data cleansing?
questions.explanation: The module lists handling missing data, reducing noisy data, and identifying/removing duplicates as data-cleansing techniques.
choices: Identify and sort out missing data
correctAnswers: Identify and sort out missing data

questions.question: Which activity belongs to feature engineering rather than data cleansing in the module?
questions.explanation: Feature encoding is listed under feature engineering; missing-data handling and duplicate removal are listed under data cleansing.
questions.correctAnswer: Feature encoding

questions.question: Which EDA activity examines relationships between variables?
questions.explanation: The EDA section names correlation analysis as the activity used to examine relationships between variables.
questions.correctAnswer: Correlation analysis

questions.question: (Choose 4) Which activities are explicitly listed as EDA activities?
questions.explanation: The module lists visualization, summary statistics, outlier detection, correlation analysis, and hypothesis testing as EDA activities; four of those appear among the choices.

questions.question: The module presents preprocessing as an important step before analysis or modeling.
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly state that preprocessing is important before processing so data can be prepared for analysis or modeling.

questions.question: What does machine-learning model deployment mean in the module?
questions.explanation: Deployment is defined as taking a trained ML model and making it available for use in real-world applications.
choices: Collecting raw data before any training
Making a trained model available in real-world applications
Removing all features from a dataset
questions.correctAnswer: Making a trained model available in real-world applications

questions.question: (Choose 4) Which practices are listed for successful ML model deployment?
questions.explanation: The module lists choosing the right infrastructure, effective versioning and tracking, robust testing and validation, and monitoring and alerting.

source.section: Best Practices for Successful ML Model Deployment (p. 44)

questions.question: Why should a deployed model be continuously monitored?
questions.explanation: The module notes that real-world data can evolve and model performance can drift; monitoring detects deviations so adjustments can be made.
choices: Because training data must never be reused
Because real-world data can evolve and model performance may drift
Because monitoring removes the need for validation
Because deployed models cannot make predictions without manual input
questions.correctAnswer: Because real-world data can evolve and model performance may drift

questions.question: (Choose 5) Which principles of data ethics are presented in the module?
questions.explanation: The module presents five principles: ownership, transparency, privacy, intention, and outcomes.

source.section: Ethics and Privacy in Data Science — 5 Principles of Data Ethics (pp. 46–47)

questions.question: Which data-ethics principle emphasizes that data subjects should know how their information will be collected, stored, and used?
questions.explanation: The module defines transparency as the data subject's right to know how personal information will be collected, stored, and used.

source.section: Ethics and Privacy in Data Science — Transparency (p. 46)

questions.correctAnswer: Transparency

questions.question: According to the module, good intentions guarantee that data analysis cannot cause harm.
questions.explanation: The module explicitly notes that even with good intentions, analysis can inadvertently harm individuals or groups, described as disparate impact.

source.section: Ethics and Privacy in Data Science — Outcomes (p. 47)

questions.question: What distinguishes supervised learning in the module?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled training data containing both inputs and corresponding correct outputs.
choices: It requires manually written rules for every case
questions.correctAnswer: It uses labeled input-output examples

questions.question: Which task is a classification problem?
questions.explanation: Classification predicts categorical class labels. Filtering email into spam or not spam is one of the module's examples.
choices: Filtering email into spam or not spam
questions.correctAnswer: Filtering email into spam or not spam

questions.question: Which target type characterizes regression in the module?
questions.explanation: Regression is associated with a continuous target and prediction of real-number values.
questions.correctAnswer: Continuous real-number values

questions.question: (Choose 4) Which algorithms are listed as classification algorithms in the introductory supervised-learning section?
questions.explanation: The module lists Random Forest, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine as classification algorithms.

questions.question: Binary classification involves exactly two classes.
questions.explanation: The module defines binary classification as classification involving two classes, such as yes/no or positive/negative.

questions.question: After training and validation, what broad phase follows in the supervised-learning process shown in the module?
questions.explanation: The module describes training and validation followed by prediction on new data.
questions.correctAnswer: Prediction

questions.question: What does it mean for a supervised model to generalize?
questions.explanation: Generalization means making accurate predictions on new, unseen data with characteristics like the training data.
choices: It uses the maximum possible number of features
questions.correctAnswer: It predicts unseen data accurately

questions.question: Which pattern most strongly indicates overfitting according to the module?
questions.explanation: An overfitted model fits the training data very well but performs poorly on unseen data because it has focused too closely on training-set particularities.
choices: Poor performance on both training and unseen data
Excellent training performance but poor unseen-data performance
Equal performance on all datasets by definition
Low training performance but perfect test performance
questions.correctAnswer: Excellent training performance but poor unseen-data performance

questions.question: Which pattern describes underfitting?
questions.explanation: An underfitted model is too simple to capture the data's important variation and therefore performs poorly even on training data and also on new data.
choices: Poor performance on both training and new data
Perfect training performance and poor new-data performance
questions.correctAnswer: Poor performance on both training and new data

questions.question: (Choose 3) Which statements are supported by the module's discussion of model complexity and data?
questions.explanation: The slides relate usable complexity to input variation, note that more varied data can support more complex models, and warn that simply duplicating data does not add useful variety.

source.section: Relation of Model Complexity to Dataset Size (p. 12)

choices: Greater variety in training data can support more complex models without overfitting
Simply duplicating the same data points does not provide the needed variety
Larger and more varied datasets can permit more complex models
Model complexity is unrelated to the training data
Repeated identical samples always eliminate overfitting
correctAnswers: Greater variety in training data can support more complex models without overfitting
Simply duplicating the same data points does not provide the needed variety
Larger and more varied datasets can permit more complex models

questions.question: How does the module define variance?
questions.explanation: Variance is described as error resulting from sensitivity to noise or fluctuations in the training data.
choices: Error from sensitivity to training-data noise and fluctuations
Error caused only by missing labels
The number of classes in a dataset
questions.correctAnswer: Error from sensitivity to training-data noise and fluctuations

questions.question: The error caused by wrong or overly simple assumptions in the learning algorithm is called ____.
questions.explanation: The module defines bias as error from wrong or too-simple assumptions in the learning algorithm.

questions.question: Why is the synthetic wave dataset used in the module?
questions.explanation: The wave dataset has one input feature and a continuous target, making it an example for illustrating regression algorithms.
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate regression algorithms

questions.question: What kind of task is associated with the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset in the module?
questions.explanation: Tumors are labeled benign or malignant, and the task is to predict the class from tissue measurements, making it a classification task.
choices: Classification of tumors as benign or malignant
questions.correctAnswer: Classification of tumors as benign or malignant

questions.question: In the extended housing example, what does the module call the creation of derived inputs such as products between original features?
questions.explanation: The slides call the inclusion of derived features such as feature interactions 'feature engineering.'
questions.correctAnswer: Feature engineering

questions.question: How does k-nearest-neighbors classification assign a label when k is greater than one?
questions.explanation: The module explains that k-NN counts the classes among the selected neighbors and assigns the majority class.
choices: By majority voting among the k nearest neighbors
By averaging all feature values in the dataset
By selecting the farthest training point
By building a hierarchy of if/else tests
questions.correctAnswer: By majority voting among the k nearest neighbors

questions.question: (Choose 2) Which are identified as important k-NN classifier parameters?
questions.explanation: The module highlights the number of neighbors and the distance measure as two important k-NN classifier parameters.

questions.question: What happens to nearest-neighbor regression predictions as more neighbors are considered, according to the module's comparison?
questions.explanation: The module notes that more neighbors produce smoother, less complex predictions that fit the training data less closely.
choices: They always pass through every training point
They stop depending on neighboring samples
questions.correctAnswer: They generally become smoother

questions.question: What is the effect of increasing alpha in ridge regression according to the module?
questions.explanation: A higher alpha imposes stronger restriction, resulting in coefficients with smaller magnitudes.
choices: It forces every coefficient to increase
questions.correctAnswer: It makes coefficient magnitudes smaller

questions.question: What characteristic of lasso coefficients is emphasized in the module?
questions.explanation: The lasso example shows that regularization can drive many coefficients exactly to zero, with stronger regularization producing smaller and sparser coefficients.
choices: Every coefficient must increase with alpha
questions.correctAnswer: Many coefficients can become zero

questions.question: For LogisticRegression and LinearSVC, what does a higher value of C mean in the module?
questions.explanation: The module states that higher C corresponds to less regularization and greater emphasis on fitting individual training points correctly.
questions.correctAnswer: Less regularization

questions.question: A low value of C in LogisticRegression or LinearSVC places more emphasis on a coefficient vector close to zero.
questions.explanation: The module states that low C increases the emphasis on finding a coefficient vector close to zero.

questions.question: How does a decision tree make a prediction for a new data point?
questions.explanation: A point is routed from the root through tests until it reaches a region/leaf, where the target associated with that region is predicted.
choices: By traversing tests from the root to the appropriate region or leaf
By averaging every target in the entire dataset regardless of features
questions.correctAnswer: By traversing tests from the root to the appropriate region or leaf

questions.question: (Choose 3) Which statements about decision trees are supported by the module?
questions.explanation: The module describes trees as hierarchies of if/else tests, identifies the top node as the root, and notes that scikit-learn provides classifier and regressor implementations.

source.section: Decision Trees; Building Decision Trees; Decision Trees in Scikit-learn

choices: They learn a hierarchy of if/else questions
The top node is called the root
They require Euclidean distance for every split
correctAnswers: They learn a hierarchy of if/else questions
The top node is called the root

questions.question: Which limitation of decision-tree regression is explicitly noted in the module?
questions.explanation: The module notes that decision-tree regression cannot extrapolate predictions outside the range represented by the training data.
choices: It cannot extrapolate outside the training-data range
It requires all features to be categorical
questions.correctAnswer: It cannot extrapolate outside the training-data range

questions.question: What is a bootstrap sample in the random-forest construction described in the module?
questions.explanation: A bootstrap sample is built by drawing n_samples examples randomly with replacement, producing a dataset the same size as the original with some repeated and some omitted observations.
choices: A sample drawn randomly with replacement to the original sample size
A sample containing each observation exactly once
A sample consisting only of misclassified examples
A sample created by removing every duplicate
questions.correctAnswer: A sample drawn randomly with replacement to the original sample size

questions.question: (Choose 3) Which statements describe random forests in the module?
questions.explanation: Random forests combine multiple decision trees, inject randomness through data and feature selection, and aggregate tree predictions.
choices: They inject randomness into tree construction
They aggregate predictions from multiple trees
They consist of a single unpruned tree
They require every tree to use identical samples and feature choices
correctAnswers: They inject randomness into tree construction
They aggregate predictions from multiple trees

questions.question: The module states that random forests generally do not require data scaling.
questions.explanation: In its listed advantages, the module notes that random forests have no data-scale requirement.

source.section: Random Forests — Strengths, Weaknesses, and Parameters

questions.question: How does gradient boosting build successive trees according to the module?
questions.explanation: The module describes each new shallow tree as compensating for errors made by the previous trees.
choices: Each new tree is built to compensate for previous errors
Every tree is an identical copy of the first
Trees are created without reference to previous errors
Only one tree is ever trained
questions.correctAnswer: Each new tree is built to compensate for previous errors

questions.question: (Choose 3) Which parameters are highlighted for gradient boosting?
questions.explanation: The module lists n_estimators, learning rate, and max_depth as important gradient-boosting parameters.

source.section: Gradient Boosting — Strengths, Weaknesses, and Parameters
